analysis.one_liner: Stops brand-name drug makers from paying generic competitors to keep cheaper drugs off the market.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or floor action in either chamber.
analysis.plain_summary: Brand-name drug companies sometimes pay a generic competitor to delay launching a cheaper copy of a drug — a "pay-for-delay" deal. This bill would cut off the reward that makes those deals work: under current law, the first generic company to challenge a brand drug gets a 180-day head start on selling the generic, and the bill says any company that signs a deal to delay its generic loses that head start. It would also let other generic makers sell the drug sooner and require companies to disclose delay agreements to the government. The bill never got a hearing or vote; it sat in the Senate health committee until the session ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who take brand-name drugs facing a generic challenge: faster entry of cheaper generics means lower drug costs at the pharmacy and for insurers, which feeds back into premiums. Taxpayers also benefit through lower prices in Medicare and Medicaid. The main beneficiaries would be the generic drug companies willing to compete rather than take a settlement payment.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and taxpayers buying brand-name drugs

how_it_helps.text: It bars a generic company that agrees with the brand manufacturer to delay its generic drug from getting the 180-day exclusivity reward, removing the payoff that makes pay-for-delay deals work.
It lets other generic makers launch sooner — 30 days after the first one starts selling — so cheaper copies reach the market faster even when the first filer sits on its approval.
It requires companies to disclose the text of any agreement to delay a generic to HHS within ten business days, so regulators can see the terms instead of relying on litigation to uncover them.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would lose a tool for extending monopoly prices past their patents, and generic companies would lose the option of being paid to stay off the market. Consumers would pay less for the affected drugs.

drawbacks.text: The bill removes the 180-day exclusivity reward from a generic maker that signs a delay agreement, but the 45-day-litigation requirement could discourage some generic companies from challenging weak brand patents, since a single filed-and-settled infringement suit could complicate their eligibility.

Some brand-generic settlements are legitimate resolutions of genuine patent disputes; the bill does not distinguish between those and pay-for-delay, and treats any agreement to defer marketing as disqualifying.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the upside was large: faster generic entry on brand drugs where a company paid a generic maker to stay off the market means lower out-of-pocket drug costs. The costs are modest and mostly fall on brand manufacturers and generic companies that profit from delay deals; the requirement to notify the government of such agreements is a light compliance burden. The strongest good-faith objection is that some settlements legitimately resolve patent disputes and compensate generic makers for litigation risk, and the bill's penalty — stripping the 180-day exclusivity that rewards generic challengers — could in some cases push companies away from filing challenges at all. On balance the design targeted a specific, documented abuse while preserving the incentive structure for generic competition, though it never received a committee vote or floor debate, so its practical effects were never tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Health Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced March 7, 2013, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
That was the last action recorded: the committee never took it up, no version passed the Senate or House, and the 113th Congress ended January 3, 2015.
It carried six cosponsors from both parties, but no committee or floor vote ever occurred.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug companies keep the ability to pay generic competitors to delay cheaper drugs, preserving longer stretches of high monopoly prices. Patients and payers keep paying brand-level prices for drugs whose patents and challenges are effectively settled in private.

for.name: Sen. Al Franken
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its push to end pay-for-delay agreements.

for.name: Sen. David Vitter
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor at introduction.

for.name: Sens. Durbin, Shaheen, and Sanders, plus one more cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, bringing total cosponsor support to six senators.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 7, 2013 and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill in the two years remaining in the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — a Republican, Senator Vitter, was an original cosponsor alongside Democrats and an Independent — but with only six cosponsors it never reached the stage where party blocs took positions.

industries.note: The bill takes away their ability to pay generic competitors to stay off the market, which is how many keep monopoly pricing going after patents nominally expire. Consumers would pay less; their revenue per drug would fall.

Honest first filers gain — they can launch earlier and the reward for challenging bad patents stays with those who actually market the drug. But generic makers that profit from sitting on approved drugs under side agreements lose that payday.
